 Dead-End Job Is the Halloween K-Drama Where Rent Is the Real Monster
 November 1, 2026 by Contributor 
 Generated illustration 
 Netflix's Dead-End Job sends Lee Jae-wook into haunted workplaces for big money. Here's the cast, the scares, the shaky CGI and a 7/10 verdict before you press play. 
 A flyer pinned at the bottom of a bridge is not how most people find a job, and that’s the first red flag in Dead-End Job . Our Dead-End Job review comes down to this: the Netflix K-drama ( Kkuralba in Korean) is a spooky, funny, surprisingly pointed watch, with a few weak spots. It’s streaming now, just in time for Halloween weekend.
 The setup
 Hyuk-jun (Lee Jae-wook) is thirty, buried in debt and out of ideas. The flyer advertises Spyder Staffing Agency, which offers part-time temp work at extraordinarily high wages. The agency does everything it can to scare him off. Spiders cover an entire door frame. Its boss, Mr. S (Lee Hee-joon), knows exactly who Hyuk-jun is before they’ve spoken. There’s a vow of secrecy, and breaking it carries incredible penalties.
 Photo: Netflix 
 Hyuk-jun signs anyway. Each assignment sends him somewhere dangerous with almost no briefing, so whether he walks out depends on his wits and a bit of luck. The series is created by Han Jun-hee and directed by Kim Da-min. Reviewer Sarah Musnicky of But Why Tho, who has seen the first five episodes, describes a familiar assignment-per-episode structure.
 The cast
 Lee Jae-wook gets a workout here. Musnicky calls it possibly one of his most punishingly physical roles to date. He’s thrown around, he sprints, and at one point he climbs a hallway wall at a 90-degree angle. Yes, really. His Hyuk-jun grows more exasperated with every gig, which seems fair.
 Kim Min-ha plays his younger sister, Ji-yoon, and she may be the show’s best asset. Where her brother panics, she barely blinks. The review says her “can’t be bothered” energy makes her the person you’d want on a post-apocalypse survival team. She also gets the show’s best line of philosophy: “poverty is scarier than ghosts.”
 Lee Hee-joon gives Mr. S just enough menace that you doubt his motives at every turn. He does explain to Hyuk-jun why the business exists, but a lot is still unexplained. Go Min-si plays Yeon-joo, who presents herself as an investigator. Here the review is blunt: she’s the least developed character, in both performance and writing, and one of the weaker links so far. That’s a letdown for a name this big on the poster, though the back half of the series has time to fix it.
 The scares, the pixels and the CGI
 The show’s look starts with the opening credits, which are pixelated and, in Musnicky’s word, incredibly adorable. They’re a cute contrast to what follows, and they don’t hide the grim economics underneath.
 The assignments take place in locations that let the cast and director play with fear and comedy in turn. The first five episodes include a haunted convenience store with a deeply sketchy storage closet, a clown who delivers daytime horror, and a movie theater dripping in blood. The reviewer says the mix produces memorable scares and some hilariously jarring moments in equal measure.
 The weak point is the digital monsters. In the opening episode, practical effects work far better than the CGI creature, whose textures look too shiny and clean against grungy surroundings. It improves in episode two, where optical illusions and CGI combine to suit a trickster monster. Later episodes handle environmental effects with more finesse. The pattern is clear: when the show builds real sets and uses physical effects, you feel the fear.
 Why it sticks
 Under the haunted-house gags, the show asks whether any amount of money is worth risking your health and safety every time. It makes that question hard to dismiss. Hyuk-jun also meets an old classmate whose health has been wrecked by high-intensity labor. For that man, Spyder’s offer may be the only way to earn enough to survive.
 Musnicky argues you could swap the supernatural dangers for a real-world job that’s high-risk, labor-intensive and well paid, and the same conversation would still hold. With so many people worldwide competing in a shrinking job market, she says, that’s what makes the series feel relatable and not merely fun.
 The verdict
 Musnicky gives Dead-End Job 7/10. Her summary is that, CGI and monster-of-the-week formula aside, it’s a fun romp that’s as enjoyable as it is relatable. The brother-sister pairing is easy to root for as they scramble for a stable income in what she calls a world falling apart.
 Her review is based on five episodes, so the ending is still unjudged. She says a solid finish, plus answers about the outside forces interested in the agency, could push it toward greatness. If it doesn’t land, she says, it’s still a good time. Her other open question is whether the second half digs into Ji-yoon’s weaknesses.
 For a Halloween weekend, that’s a decent deal: a haunted-gig anthology with a sharp point about work, a hardworking lead and a clown, all streaming on Netflix since October 30.
